the phototransduction genes are expressed at the same levels in the ground squirrel and mouse retinas, with the exception of the rod transducin alpha subunit, which is expressed at lower levels in the ground squirrels.

the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying visual adaptation in the ground squirrel, an animal with an annual cycle in photopigment composition.
the molecular basis for light adaptation of photoreceptor cells.
the development and application of new methods for studying the molecular mechanisms underlying the regulation of gene expression.

the expression of the genes encoding the phototransduction proteins in the ground squirrel is similar to that of the rodent retina and is consistent with the ground squirrel being an excellent animal model for studying the molecular biology of phototransductive processes in the retina.

the retina of the ground squirrel is not only able to adapt its photoreceptor cells to the changing light intensities during the day and night but is also able to adapt the photoreceptor cells in a way to cope with the seasonal changes in light intensities.
the retina of the ground squirrel is capable of a high degree of phototransductive efficiency, as evidenced by the high levels of expression of phototransducer proteins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the retina of the ground squirrel, which has a unique adaptation to hibernation, has the ability to express phototransduction genes in a seasonal fashion.
the retina is an extremely complicated organ that contains a wide variety of cells and cell types that are involved in the process of vision.
the expression of phototransducer genes is regulated in the ground squirrel eye by photoperiod, and that this regulation occurs in the retina.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the photoreceptor cell bodies are the primary source of the phototransduction genes, but the inner nuclear and outer nuclear layers of the retina are also sources.
the phototransduction pathway is highly conserved in the ground squirrel, and that the expression of the genes in the pathway is similar to that of other mammals.
